message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is not a recent species but a much older mammalian ancestor that gave rise to two very different lineages:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra | Last common ancestor |
|-----------------|------|-------|----------------------|
| Species | Panthera leo | Equus quagga | — |
| Genus | Panthera | Equus | — |
| Family | Felidae (cats) | Equidae (horses, zebras, donkeys) | — |
| Order | Carnivora (carnivores) | Perissodactyla (odd‑toed ungulates) | **Laurasiatheria** (a super‑order of placental mammals) |
| Clade | — | — | **Laurasiatheria** – a group that includes carnivores, ungulates, bats, whales, and others. |
| Time of divergence | ~70–80 million years ago | — | The last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria lived in the late Cretaceous to early Paleogene (≈70–80 Ma). |

So, the lion and zebra share a common ancestor that was a small, insectivorous or omnivorous mammal belonging to the Laurasiatheria clade, living roughly 70–80 million years ago. This ancestor is far removed from either modern lion or zebra, but it is the most recent point at which the two lineages diverged.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Wait, lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor is a more distant mammalian ancestor, likely a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would be a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor is a mammal from the Laurasiatheria clade, likely a small, insectivorous mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. Or we can say: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a member of the Laurasiatheria clade, dating back to the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene. So answer accordingly. No tool needed.
